epilogue.title: EPILOGUE
epilogue.intro_won: The Assembly ratified your Pidato Pertanggungjawaban. For the first time in the Republic’s history, a sitting president stood before the representatives of the nation to answer for his stewardship—and prevailed not by decree or by force, but by the count of the ballot box.
epilogue.intro_lost: The Assembly rejected your Pidato Pertanggungjawaban. The defeat stung, yet the verdict was rendered in open session by seven hundred delegates, and power passed the way it must in a constitutional republic: peacefully, before dawn, under the rules.
epilogue.intro_common: You took the oath of office over a country in receivership and a capital still smelling of smoke. You leave behind an unfettered press, rival parties contending in the open, and a parliament that no longer rubber-stamps Bina Graha. What followed was not your work alone, but none of it could have begun without the doors you unbolted.

epilogue.end.caption: Jakarta, 1999–2026
epilogue.end.p1: In the history that actually transpired, the People’s Consultative Assembly voted 355 to 322 shortly after midnight on October 20, 1999—with nine abstentions and four spoiled ballots—to reject B.J. Habibie’s accountability speech. He withdrew from the presidential race before dawn. Hours later, Abdurrahman Wahid, the nearly blind Nahdlatul Ulama cleric known across the archipelago as Gus Dur, defeated Megawati Sukarnoputri 373 to 313 in the Republic’s first contested presidential election. Megawati, whose party had won the June polls, was elected vice president the following day to calm the red-shirted crowds in the streets. Whatever course the ballots took in Senayan, the larger watershed was the same: a seventeen-month caretaker presidency ended on green slips of paper counted aloud in a parliamentary hall, rather than by tanks at the gates.
epilogue.end.p2: To measure the distance traveled, one need only recall the wreckage of 1998. The rupiah, trading near 2,400 to the dollar in mid-1997, had plunged past 16,800 by June 1998. Real GDP contracted by roughly 13 percent in a single year, while inflation neared 80 percent. Suharto had signed his second letter of intent with the IMF on January 15, 1998, under the folded arms of Michel Camdessus, after the abrupt closure of sixteen banks in November 1997 triggered a systemic run. Then came the Trisakti shootings on May 12, the three days of arson and pogroms from May 13 to 15 in which over a thousand people perished in burning shopping malls and ethnic Chinese women were subjected to organized terror, and finally Suharto’s resignation on the morning of May 21 as students held the roofs of Senayan.
epilogue.end.p3: Rebuilding the financial system cost roughly Rp 658 trillion in bank recapitalization bonds—more than half a year’s GDP—driving public debt from 24 percent of GDP before the crash to nearly 93 percent. The Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency spent six years liquidating seized assets and pursuing delinquent tycoons before winding down in 2004, while four insolvent state banks were fused into Bank Mandiri in 1999. Across the IMF programs from 1997 to 2003, Jakarta drew roughly SDR 7.4 billion (around $$11.1 billion). In 2006, riding a commodity boom and tighter fiscal discipline, the administration of Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono paid down $$3.75 billion in June and cleared the remaining $$3.2 billion that October, four years ahead of the December 2010 schedule, before dissolving the World Bank-led Consultative Group on Indonesia in January 2007. Indonesia exited the decade owing the Fund nothing and growing at over 5 percent a year.
epilogue.end.p4: Between 1999 and 2002, the MPR amended the 1945 Constitution four times: capping presidents at two terms, establishing direct presidential elections, creating the Constitutional Court, and phasing out the military’s appointed legislative seats by 2004. Regional autonomy took effect on January 1, 2001, followed by direct local elections for governors, regents, and mayors in 2005. The Press Law of September 1999 buried the old SIUPP licensing regime for good, returning Tempo, Detik, and Editor to the newsstands, while the Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK), established in 2002, spent its first decade putting cabinet ministers, central bankers, and police generals behind bars.
epilogue.end.p5: In East Timor, 78.5 percent of voters rejected autonomy within Indonesia on August 30, 1999. Army-backed militias torched Dili and displaced hundreds of thousands before Australian-led INTERFET peacekeepers under Major General Peter Cosgrove came ashore on September 20. The MPR ratified the separation that October, and Timor-Leste raised its flag as an independent nation on May 20, 2002.
epilogue.end.p6: Peace in Aceh came out of catastrophe. After the Indian Ocean tsunami of December 26, 2004 claimed some 170,000 lives across the province, former Finnish president Martti Ahtisaari brokered the Helsinki Memorandum of Understanding between Jakarta and the Free Aceh Movement on August 15, 2005. Earlier accords at Malino had quieted the sectarian bloodshed in Poso and Ambon, even as the Bali bombings of October 12, 2002 underscored the rise of militant networks. Yet impunity endured: no senior commander answered in court for May 1998, disappeared activists such as Wiji Thukul were never found, and Suharto died on January 27, 2008 without ever standing trial.
epilogue.end.p7: Habibie lived to witness two decades of the order he helped usher in. He established The Habibie Center in 1999 to champion democratization and scientific advancement, and passed away on September 11, 2019, at the age of 83—having seen Yudhoyono win re-election in 2009 and Joko Widodo, a former furniture exporter from Surakarta from outside the old Jakarta establishment, win the presidency in 2014.
epilogue.end.p8: Yet the struggle over Reformasi’s legacy never truly closed. In September 2019, days after Habibie’s passing, parliament revised the KPK statute over massive student protests. In February 2024, Prabowo Subianto—Suharto’s former son-in-law, whose removal from Kostrad command in May 1998 defined the opening hours of Habibie’s presidency—won the presidency in a landslide and took the oath on October 20, 2024, twenty-five years to the day after Gus Dur. In March 2025, parliament unanimously expanded the civilian posts open to active-duty officers under a revised Armed Forces Law, and in August 2025 demonstrations convulsed more than a hundred cities after 21-year-old ride-hailing driver Affan Kurniawan was killed beneath a police tactical vehicle. Human Rights Watch’s 2026 assessment highlighted the renewed encroachment of the military into civilian governance—yet across the archipelago, an unruly press and a generation born after 1998 continued to contest the streets, refusing to surrender the republic Habibie’s brief caretaker presidency had pried open.
